## TL;DR

Round-one review found three connected gaps in the 401 response flow: the sign-in alert appeared with an empty-project creation prompt, cached environment/key metadata remained visible after authorization failed, and create/editor mutation paths could display the raw “Authentication required” response. I updated the Secrets view so any 401 clears its environment and key page cache, hides the stale ledger and management controls, and shows fixed sign-in guidance. The empty-project state is gated on authorization failure, while other refresh failures preserve their existing cached-empty behavior. Environment creation and editor-open now use the same fixed 401 message. The strengthened UI suite passes, and the required changed-path check is green.

## Work and rationale

I re-read the latest review findings and checked RepoOS state before editing. The live board listed #1164 as active, so the reviewed branch was available for fixes without a status transition.

The first correction was to separate an authentication failure from an empty project. The sign-in alert and the “Give this project an environment” action must not appear together: a user whose request was rejected cannot successfully create an environment. The empty-state section is now suppressed while the page is in its 401 state, and the New environment button is gated by the same state even if the client auth store still has an admin role from before a session expired.

I also treated a 401 after a warm cache as a boundary change. Previously the page could retain a stale key inventory and show only “Refresh failed,” which left old project metadata on screen after the server denied access. The 401 handler now clears the selected environment, environment list, current snapshot and cached `project-environments` / `secrets:*` entries. It hides the ledger and replaces any stale refresh state with the sign-in alert. This keeps warm-cache behavior consistent with a cold unauthenticated request and reduces the chance of displaying metadata after a session expires.

The shared `safeError` branch now handles 401 by setting the fixed sign-in message and clearing cached state. The create-environment and open-in-editor catches had bypassed that branch by directly showing `ApiError.message`, so they now route 401 through the same fixed guidance. Other API errors retain their prior useful message behavior; non-API create failures continue to use the generic safe fallback.

The regression tests now use the actual server response text, “Authentication required.” The cold 401 case checks the sign-in alert, absence of both creation affordances, and absence of raw server text. A warm-cache case first renders the existing admin-role key list, then rejects the environment refresh with 401 and verifies that the ledger, key name, empty-project CTA, and new-environment button disappear. Separate mutation tests exercise 401 from environment creation and editor-open, checking that neither the dialog nor toast exposes the raw body. Existing admin-role tests continue to exercise the successful populated UI, while the write-only value tests remain in place.

## Approaches tried

I initially gated the empty state on any error. The existing cached-empty refresh test showed that this changed unrelated offline behavior: a previously known empty project should retain its empty-state context when a background refresh fails for a non-auth reason. I narrowed the gate to the specific 401 state, which fixes the misleading unauthorized CTA without changing ordinary refresh-error behavior.

I then added an explicit warm-cache regression instead of relying only on the cold 401 test. It confirmed that invalidating the environment and `secrets:` cache prefix prevents stale metadata from surviving the denial. I also tested the mutation paths independently because they do not pass through the page-load catch handler.

## Challenges and blockers

The first scoped check after implementation caught a formatting failure in the Vue template. I ran `bun run fmt` as required, then reran the complete scoped check. The final run passed remote build and tests, plus local format, lint, build-staleness, CSS/theme checks, contrast audit and UI smoke.

As recorded in the prior draft, live browser access was unavailable in this environment. The computer-use browser host did not expose a browser session, so authenticated success is still evidenced by the admin-role UI harness and its API doubles rather than a live login and server round trip. The 401 response handling is tested against the real server message text but also through the UI test harness.

## Key learnings

A 401 must be handled consistently across page reads and mutations. Fixing only the main list request leaves alternate actions able to leak server-auth text or preserve stale state. Centralizing the 401 behavior and adding tests for each call path makes the rule easier to preserve.

Warm caches need explicit authorization semantics. Keeping stale data is useful during ordinary connectivity failures, but an authorization denial is different: the view should clear cached project metadata and stop offering actions that the server will reject.

Finally, UI review evidence should map to the state being reviewed. The earlier populated fixture demonstrates the signed-in-role presentation but bypasses the environment API, so it is not evidence of a server-authenticated round trip or of the changed unsigned state. Those limits remain explicit rather than overstating what the browser or test harness observed.
